The management has relied upon the judgments of Man sukh Lal (supra), where the Hon'ble Supreme Court in 1997 addressed the issue of home guards who were aggrieved by their discharge/termination from service.

The court ruled against the right to reinstatement and regularization of home guards, holding that the Homeguards are fundamentally a volunteer organization, not an "employment" or "source of employment".

It was noted that Homeguards can come from various walks of life, including government and private sector employees, professionals, industrial workers, students, and others willing to dedicate their spare time for community service.
The court maintained that regularizing volunteers or their activities would undermine the essential voluntary ethos and character of the Homeguards.

Likewise, reliance is also placed upon Rajesh Mishra & Ors.
vs. Govt. of NCT of Delhi, 2002 (3) LLN 669, Grah Rakshak, Homeguards Welfare Association vs.
State of H.P. & Ors., Civil Appeal No. 2759 of 2015 (SLP (C) No. 12858 of 2009).
31.
This tribunal has gone through the aforesaid judgements cited by the management and is of the considered opinion that the same are not applicable to the present case.
In the present case, there is a difference between the service conditions of the claimants and that of petitioners in previous judgments, such as the Mansukh Lal(Supra) case.
Earlier decisions were in the context of Homeguards Volunteers who were performing their duties in line with the mission and vision of the Bombay Home Guards Act.
In the present case, the claimants, although categorized as "Homeguards", have been performing permanent and perennial duties across various departments at the behest of the management.
Their responsibilities bear no relation to the emergency call-out duties outlined in the Act.
Instead, they are required to work 8 hours a day, 7 days a week, and 365 days a year, often performing double duties on several occasions of national importance.

32. As far as the question of "voluntariness" is concerned, once the claimants are enrolled as Homeguards, they are mandated to comply with every order assigned by their superior officers as stipulated in Rule 14 of the Delhi Home Guards Ru
Failure to comply subjects them to penalties for neglect or refusal to obey orders, as specified in Sections 6 and 7 of the Bombay Home Guards Act, 1947, as extended to the Union Territory of Delhi.

Thus, the workers are compelled Rajender Kumar And 1432 Ors vs The Management Of Directorate Of Home ... on 12 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/96818398/
12 under all circumstances to perform various duties--whether a
The routine work and daily duty hours they are required to fulfill effectively preclude them from securing any other employment.
Specifically, if an individual is tasked with driving duties for 8 hours a day, every day of the year, it is impossible for them to engage in any other gainful employment.
33. The claimants have performed duties typically reserved for regular Class-IV and Class-III employees such as drivers, data entry operators, and multi-tasking staff for up to 15 years.
Their 8-hour daily shifts, including weekends and holidays, sometimes even double shifts, render it impossible for them to hold other jobs.
This continuous deployment contradicts the core purpose of the Homeguards, which is to provide emergency support, not regular employment.
The management has not demonstrated that these workers were ever called for emergency duties as envisioned by the Bombay Home Guards Act over the past 15 years.
Hence, the reliance of the management upon the Bombay Home Guards Act and Rules and the aforesaid judgements will not be of any help.
Considering these prevailing circumstances, this Tribunal is constrained to lift the veil of "voluntary service" created by the management.

Once the veil of "volunteer service" created by the management is pierced, then it emerges that there exists a relationship of master-servant or employer-employee between the management and the claimants.

34. In my considered opinion after going through the evidence placed on record by both the parties this tribunal has arrived at a conclusion that the claimants herein are indeed the "workman" as defined under section 2(s) of the I.D. Act.
They have been performing the manual and unskilled/skilled nature of duties of Driver, MTS, DEO etc. (as outlined above) for the past 15 years continuously and uninterruptedly.
They were duly selected pursuant to the selection process conducted by the selection board of the management and were deployed at various agencies for performing the said work.
Despite performing the regular nature of duties under the control and supervision of the management, they were not recognised as "workers" or "employees" but were treated merely as "volunteers".
The management, under the guise of categorizing claimants "Homeguard volunteers", has denied them the status of "employees".
They were required to work relentlessly i.e. 8 hours daily, without a single paid leave of Sundays, gazetted holidays, and festivals such as Holi and Diwali.
On these occasions, they were often asked to perform double round the clock duties.
It is also reiterated that while performing overtime-round the clock duties, they were not given wages in accordance with the overtime rates as prescribed under the law.

Meaning thereby, these so-called volunteers are working day-in and day-out more than the permanent employees working in the establishment of management employed by the management, and paid "duty allowances" on a monthly basis.

We have called for the data in the instant case to ensure as to how many employees were working on contract basis or ad-hoc basis or daily-wage basis in different State departments.

This situation was not envisaged by Uma Devi (supra).
